A1.justification: Both complete, readable PDFs describe the same QMV/EDFL/ISR framework and three experiments. Their equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–H support comparison despite substantial rewriting and layout changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original permutation experiments on 3,059 items, randomized support-dose results, and a 528-item Gemma-2-9B audit.

after.justification: v2 retains original dispersion, mixture, dose-response, and held-out audit outcomes, including numerical results in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 specializes v1's output-level log-ratio budget to KL(Ber(p_ref) || Ber(q_k)). This changes the general computation, although supervised point-mass references reduce to the same negative log-likelihood. The permutation-mixture ISR gate remains, while v1's proposed training-time logit-variance regularizer and graduated refuse/hedge policy are omitted.

E1.justification: Both use the same 3,059-item Factuality Slice assembled from FEVER, HotpotQA, NQ-Open, PopQA, and Controls, with the same dose experiment and held-out audit. Controls already appear in v1 Appendix H; describing the collection as five benchmarks does not add coverage. New deployment examples are not evaluated tasks.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparisons retain single-permutation predictions, uniform mixtures, globally optimized convex mixtures, and the oracle single-permutation comparator. Appendix C's comparison table matches between v1 Table 2 and v2 Table 4. Newly cited selective-classification methods are not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: For Qwen2-7B dispersion evaluation, v1 Section 4.1.1 specifies 12 permutations, whereas v2 Section 4.2.1 specifies 16; Llama remains at 16. The separate mixture analysis already used 16 in v1. This is a reported protocol revision without evidence establishing reruns; the retained splits, dose arms, and audit settings otherwise match.

E4.justification: v2 removes the permutation-skeleton ablation reported in v1 Section 4.3, including slopes of 0.245 for three bands and 0.291 for uniform permutations. The permutation-count/clipping sensitivity table, IV robustness discussion, conditional-independence audit, and rare-event analysis remain in the appendices.

E5.justification: v2 Section 4.1 newly specifies Wilson intervals for proportions and OLS slope confidence intervals over 58 depth-level means, and discloses fine-tuning seed 42. It removes v1's audit Jensen-gap interval [0.71, 0.93], retaining the 0.82 estimate. No increase in repeated training runs is established.

E6.justification: The central dose–budget relationship reverses: v1 reports a 0.375-nat increase per support chunk and correlation +0.80; v2 reports a 0.375-nat decrease and correlation −0.80, interpreting the 0.127 hallucination reduction per nat of decrease. This substantively changes a central empirical relationship. The dose≈1 accuracy crossover and permutation-skeleton results disappear, while the 17.6-point hallucination reduction and principal mixture/audit scores remain.

T1.justification: v2 Sections 3.1 and 3.4 explicitly define predicate-level reference distributions and the average Bernoulli-KL budget, with a data-processing inequality relating it to the full-distribution budget. This adds a limited formal specialization. The principal QMV, MDL, and EDFL formulas and Appendix A proofs are otherwise retained.

C1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion narrow the contribution from a unified explanation of why language models hallucinate to order sensitivity and information budgeting for evidence-grounded binary adjudication. Bayes-optimality becomes a qualified possibility, and EDFL is presented as an actionable Bernoulli specialization. QMV, EDFL, and ISR remain the central components.

C2.justification: v2 explains that mixture realizability does not establish implementation by standard transformers or recovery through SGD. It explicitly acknowledges that the required reference may be unavailable before answering and makes deployment guarantees conditional on verification and verifier error. These qualifications replace v1's stronger deterministic compression-failure interpretation and broad assertions about positional encodings satisfying the assumptions.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands reproducibility documentation: Section 4.1 supplies the Gemma LoRA configuration, learning rate, epoch, batching, precision, and schedule, while Table 1 accounts for forward passes. Appendix H adds inclusion criteria and clarifies source counts as pre-filter sampling caps. Code and data links remain withheld, with release promised at camera-ready. These are disclosures, not established changes to training.

R1.justification: v1's claim to the first predictive compression-failure theory is replaced by explicit recognition that EDFL follows immediately from KL convexity and data processing. v2 repositions the contribution around Bernoulli decision rules and connects it to reject-option classification and risk–coverage tradeoffs, adding Chow (1970) and Geifman and El-Yaniv (2017).

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contributions, related work, and discussion are extensively rewritten. Experiments adopt a Question/Design/Results structure, and new conceptual and deployment explanations reshape the narrative. The title and author line change, and the worked example moves from the main text to Appendix B.3.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main paper from one column to two and adds three figures displaying dispersion/mixture summaries, dose-response, and the audit operating point. It adds compute and dataset-composition tables, reformats the retained results tables, and relocates the worked example. The figures primarily visualize existing reported evidence.

improvement.justification: v2 improves transparency through narrower claims, explicit reference/verifier requirements, the conceptual qualification of mixture realizability, and substantially better fine-tuning and dataset documentation. These gains support a limited overall improvement despite the removed ablation and Jensen-gap interval. Most experimental evidence remains unchanged, and the dose–budget sign reversal is not explained as a correction or new analysis, limiting confidence in a larger improvement.
